title: Type of Triangle
notes:
## Intuition

The triangle test says each side must be shorter than the sum of the other two. Checking all three inequalities works, but after sorting the sides as `a <= b <= c` only one can fail: `a + c > b` and `b + c > a` hold automatically because `c` is the largest. Sorting also lines up equal lengths next to each other, so the type is decided by comparing neighbours.

## Approach

1. Copy `nums`, sort it ascending and name the sides `a`, `b`, `c`.
2. If `a + b <= c`, the sides cannot close up into a triangle: return `"none"`.
3. If `a === c`, the smallest and largest are equal, so all three are: return `"equilateral"`.
4. If `a === b` or `b === c`, exactly two match: return `"isosceles"`.
5. Otherwise return `"scalene"`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 3, 3]` sorts to `a = 3, b = 3, c = 3`. `3 + 3 = 6` is greater than `3`, so it is a triangle. `a === c`, so the answer is `"equilateral"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1): sorting three values and a few comparisons.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- The inequality is strict: `[1, 2, 3]` gives a flat shape, so it is `"none"`, not `"scalene"`.
- Check for `"none"` before the equal-sides tests: `[5, 5, 10]` has two equal sides but is still not a triangle.
- Sort numerically with `(x, y) => x - y`; the default sort compares as text and puts `100` before `9`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `a` | the shortest side |
| `b` | the middle side |
| `c` | the longest side |

narration.2: Sort a copy so that a is the shortest side and c the longest.
narration.3: Only the two shorter sides can fail to reach past the longest one.
narration.4: Then the lengths cannot form a triangle.
narration.6: If the shortest equals the longest, all three sides are equal.
narration.9: Otherwise, equal neighbours in sorted order mean exactly two sides match.
narration.12: All three sides differ, so the triangle is scalene.
